metadata.title: Welcome to Aptitude
metadata.description: A short, friendly introduction to numbers, calculation speed and the purpose of this foundation topic.

content.text:
Before we start solving aptitude questions, let's make one thing easier: numbers.

You don't need to be a maths genius for aptitude.

You just need to become comfortable looking at numbers and spotting simple patterns.

Quick question.

Which sounds more useful in an aptitude exam?

inlineData.prompt: Which sounds more useful in an aptitude exam?
inlineData.explanation: Exactly. Formulas matter, but recognizing the pattern first can save you much more time.

content.text:
You already do mental calculation every day.

₹500 with a 10% discount?

You probably know the answer is ₹450 without writing anything down.

If a friend says, 'We have 300 rupees and three people,' you instantly know 100 each.

Aptitude is largely about turning more of these little calculations into habits.

And that's what we're going to build here.

Not complicated maths.

Just useful shortcuts, patterns and number sense.

Ready?

We'll start very simply:

1. Basic calculations
2. BODMAS
3. Fast multiplication and division
4. Squares and cubes
5. Useful fraction, decimal and percentage values
6. Estimation and mental calculation
7. Unit conversion

By the end, numbers should feel much less intimidating.

That's our starting point.

Next, we'll begin with something very simple: the calculations you use everywhere.

We'll see how to make them faster without doing anything complicated.

Next up: Basic Arithmetic Operations.

Formulas are easy to forget under time pressure. But when you recognize patterns, math starts making sense naturally without memorizing dozens of tricks.

Let us see this in real life:

metadata.title: The Four Basics
metadata.description: Build confidence with addition, subtraction, multiplication and division.

content.text:
Let's start with the four things behind almost every aptitude calculation:

Addition
Subtraction
Multiplication
Division

Nothing fancy yet.

Addition is simply combining quantities.

27 + 13

Instead of counting everything from 27, break 13 into 10 + 3.

27 + 10 = 37
37 + 3 = 40

Small habit. Big difference.

Quick one:

48 + 17 = ?

For subtraction, rounding can help.

For example:

83 - 29

Think:
83 - 30 = 53
then add 1 back.

Answer = 54.

Try this mentally:

72 - 19 = ?

Multiplication is repeated addition, but in aptitude we want faster ways.

For example:

25 × 4

25 × 4 = 100

Easy.

And there are lots of numbers with useful mental patterns. We'll learn those properly in the next few lessons.

Division is asking:

'How many times does this number fit?'

For example:

120 ÷ 10 = 12

Once multiplication becomes familiar, division becomes much easier too.

One last one:

25 × 8 = ?

That's enough for the basics.

The goal isn't to do huge calculations in your head.
It's to notice little shortcuts wherever you can.

Next, we'll learn something that prevents one of the most common mistakes in aptitude:

What should be calculated first?

Next up: BODMAS & Order of Operations.

Let us make addition easier mentally:

Break 17 into 10 + 7.
First add 10:
48 + 10 = 58.
Now add the remaining 7:
58 + 7 = 65.

Breaking numbers into chunks removes the stress! Try this one:

Try this one using the same breakdown:

37 + 25 = ?

Here is the mental shortcut:

Instead of subtracting 19 all at once, round it up to 20!
72 - 20 = 52.

Since 19 is 1 less than 20, you subtracted 1 too many! So add 1 back:
52 + 1 = 53.

Let us practice that trick with another problem:

Try this one mentally:

64 - 19 = ?

Remember the 25 benchmark: 25 × 4 = 100.
Since 8 is 4 × 2, we just double 100 to get 200!

Try this one:

Try this one:

25 × 6 = ?

metadata.title: What Gets Calculated First?
metadata.description: Learn the correct order of operations and avoid common calculation mistakes.

content.text:
Here's a small trap.

Suppose you see:

2 + 3 × 4

Do you add first?

If you did, you'd get 20.

But the correct answer is 14.

Why?

Because multiplication is done before addition.

This is where BODMAS helps.

B — Brackets
O — Orders / powers
D — Division
M — Multiplication
A — Addition
S — Subtraction

You don't need to fear the word. It's simply a priority list.

What should happen first?

10 + 5 × 2

One detail that helps:

Division and multiplication have the same priority.

Addition and subtraction also have the same priority.

When operations have the same priority, work from left to right.

Example:

20 ÷ 5 × 2

20 ÷ 5 = 4
4 × 2 = 8

What is:

18 - 6 ÷ 3 ?

And brackets always get attention first.

(5 + 3) × 2

First:
5 + 3 = 8

Then:
8 × 2 = 16

That's BODMAS.

Nothing mysterious — just a clear order.

Next, we'll make multiplication and division faster.

You'll start seeing tricks that save you from doing the full calculation every time.

Multiplication and division always have higher priority than addition and subtraction. In 10 + 5 × 2, calculate 5 × 2 = 10 first, then 10 + 10 = 20.

Let us check this one:
In 14 - 3 × 4, what gets calculated first?

Divide first! 6 ÷ 3 = 2. Now subtract: 18 - 2 = 16. If you did 18 - 6 first, you got tripped up by the order of operations!

Try this one:
What is: 20 - 8 ÷ 2 ?

metadata.title: Multiply Faster
metadata.description: Learn simple mental multiplication and division shortcuts.

content.text:
This one is fun.

We're going to make multiplication look less like multiplication.

×5 has an easy shortcut.

Multiply by 10, then divide by 2.

Example:

36 × 5

36 × 10 = 360
360 ÷ 2 = 180

Done.

×9 is also friendly.

×9 = ×10 - the original number.

27 × 9
= 270 - 27
= 243

For small two-digit numbers, ×11 can often be done mentally.

Example:

23 × 11

23 + 230 = 253

So 23 × 11 = 253.

Division can use the same idea.

If:

480 ÷ 5

think:
480 ÷ 10 = 48
then ×2

Answer = 96

Which is easiest to calculate mentally?

48 × 25

inlineData.prompt:
Which is easiest to calculate mentally?

48 × 25
inlineData.explanation: Exactly. The trick is to recognize the useful number, not to do more arithmetic.

content.text:
A few shortcuts already make a big difference:

×5 → ×10 ÷2
×25 → ×100 ÷4
×50 → ×100 ÷2
×9 → ×10 − number

Next we're going after some numbers you'll use again and again.

Squares, cubes and a few common values. Once you know them, some questions become almost instant.

Multiplying by 5 is simply multiplying by 10 and halving!
48 × 10 = 480, and half of 480 is 240.

Try this one with the same rule:
Try this: 36 × 5 = ?

25 is 100 ÷ 4. So divide by 4 and add two zeros! 12 ÷ 4 = 3, add two zeros = 300.

Try this one:
48 ÷ 4 = 12, so 48 × 25 is instantly 1,200! Dividing by 4 is much faster mentally than multiplying by 20 and then by 5.

metadata.title: Numbers Worth Knowing
metadata.description: Build a small mental library of useful squares, cubes and common values.

content.text:
Some numbers are worth remembering.

Not because memorizing is exciting...

but because knowing them saves time everywhere.

Start with squares.

Try becoming comfortable with:

1² = 1
2² = 4
3² = 9
4² = 16
5² = 25
6² = 36
7² = 49
8² = 64
9² = 81
10² = 100

Then gradually extend to 20², 25² and 30².

Quick one.

15² = ?

Here's a useful shortcut for numbers ending in 5.

15²

Take the first digit: 1
Add 1: 2
Multiply: 1 × 2 = 2
Then put 25 at the end.

225.

So:

25² = 625
35² = 1225
45² = 2025

You don't need to memorize huge cubes.

Just get comfortable with the small ones:

1³ = 1
2³ = 8
3³ = 27
4³ = 64
5³ = 125
6³ = 216
7³ = 343
8³ = 512
9³ = 729
10³ = 1000

We'll also gradually remember useful values like:

√4 = 2
√9 = 3
√16 = 4
√25 = 5
√36 = 6
√49 = 7
√64 = 8
√81 = 9
√100 = 10

These become useful shortcuts later.

You don't need to memorize everything in one sitting.

The useful numbers will come back again and again, and repetition will make them stick.

Next, we'll connect three things you have definitely seen before:

fractions, decimals and percentages.

Once they start looking like the same thing in different clothes, aptitude gets much easier.

For any number ending in 5, multiply the tens digit by the next integer (1 × 2 = 2) and append 25 -> 225!

Let us practice:
Try this: 25² = ?

metadata.title: Three Ways to Say the Same Thing
metadata.description: Connect fractions, decimals and percentages so that conversions become almost automatic.

content.text:
Here's a useful idea:

A fraction, decimal and percentage can describe the SAME quantity.

For example:

1/2 = 0.5 = 50%

Three different ways.
Same value.

A few values are worth knowing instantly:

1/2 = 50%
1/4 = 25%
3/4 = 75%
1/5 = 20%
1/10 = 10%
1/20 = 5%
1/25 = 4%
1/8 = 12.5%

These show up everywhere.

Without calculating on paper:

What is 25% as a fraction?

inlineData.explanation: Exactly. 25% means 25 out of 100, which simplifies to 1/4.

content.text:
Percentages can also make calculations easier.

50% of a number = half
25% = one quarter
10% = divide by 10
5% = half of 10%
1% = divide by 100

For example:

25% of 80

Just take one quarter.

80 ÷ 4 = 20.

This connection becomes very important later.

A question may give you a fraction.
Another may give you a percentage.
Another may use a decimal.

But underneath, they may all be asking about the same quantity.

Once you start seeing that, many questions become much simpler.

Nice. You now have a small mental dictionary:

1/2 → 50%
1/4 → 25%
1/5 → 20%
1/10 → 10%
1/20 → 5%

Next we'll work on one of the most useful aptitude habits:

getting close to an answer quickly instead of calculating everything exactly.

Percent means per hundred. 25% = 25/100. Divide both by 25: 25/100 = 1/4.

Now look at how this simplifies calculations:

20% is 1/5! 150 ÷ 5 = 30. Alternatively, 10% is 15, so 20% is 15 × 2 = 30.

Try this one:

metadata.title: Think Fast, Calculate Less
metadata.description: Learn estimation, rounding and mental calculation habits used to save time.

content.text:
Here's a habit that can save you a surprising amount of time:

Don't calculate more than the question requires.

Suppose the options are:

498
502
750
1200

and your calculation gives you something around 500.

You don't need to spend another minute finding the last decimal place.

You already know which answer makes sense.

Which is closest to:

49 × 19?

inlineData.explanation: Exactly. 50 × 20 is 1000, so 49 × 19 should be a little below 1000. 900 is the closest option.

content.text:
A simple estimation habit:

Make one number easy first.

For example:

198 × 5

Think:
200 × 5 = 1000
Then subtract 2 × 5 = 10

Answer = 990.

Which is closest to:

397 ÷ 8?

You can estimate fractions too.

49/100 is almost 1/2.

199/400 is almost 1/2.

And 1/3 is about 0.333.

The point isn't to replace exact calculation.

It's to quickly understand the size of an answer.

A few habits to keep:

• Round when the exact number isn't necessary.
• Look at the answer options before doing heavy calculation.
• Break numbers into friendly pieces.
• Use known percentages and fractions.
• Ask yourself, 'Does this answer even make sense?'

That's a big part of aptitude: knowing when to calculate, and when not to.

One final foundation remains.

Units.

Minutes, hours, metres, kilometres, grams, kilograms...

They look simple, but mixing them up can ruin an otherwise correct solution.

Next: Unit Conversion.
Round each number: 49 is almost 50, and 19 is almost 20. 50 × 20 = 1,000. So the answer is slightly less than 1,000 -> 900 to 950!
Round 397 to 400! 400 ÷ 8 = 50. Fast rounding gives you the answer instantly without long division.

metadata.title: Don't Let Units Trick You
metadata.description: Learn the common unit conversions needed before moving into serious aptitude arithmetic.

content.text:
You've probably seen this happen:

The calculation is correct...

but the units don't match.

And suddenly the answer is wrong.

So let's make the common conversions automatic.

Length:

1 kilometre = 1000 metres
1 metre = 100 centimetres
1 centimetre = 10 millimetres

Easy rule:

Moving to a smaller unit → number gets bigger.

Moving to a larger unit → number gets smaller.
2.5 km = ? metres

Time:

1 hour = 60 minutes
1 minute = 60 seconds
1 day = 24 hours

A common aptitude conversion:

1 hour = 3600 seconds.
2.5 hours = ? minutes

inlineData.explanation: Yep. 2 hours = 120 minutes and half an hour = 30 minutes. Total = 150.

content.text:
Mass:

1 kilogram = 1000 grams
1 gram = 1000 milligrams

So:

2 kg = 2000 g
500 g = 0.5 kg

One especially important conversion comes later in Time, Speed & Distance:

1 m/s = 18/5 km/h

and

1 km/h = 5/18 m/s

You don't need to memorize why yet.

You'll use these when we reach speed and distance.

And that's the end of your first foundation topic. 🎉

You started with basic calculations and now you can:

• calculate more comfortably
• follow BODMAS
• use simple multiplication shortcuts
• recognize useful squares and cubes
• connect fractions, decimals and percentages
• estimate instead of over-calculating
• handle common unit conversions

But this was only the warm-up.

Next we're going to look at numbers themselves — factors, multiples, divisibility, HCF, LCM, remainders and some surprisingly useful tricks.

That's where aptitude starts getting interesting.

Next topic:

NUMBER SYSTEM.
1 hour = 60 minutes. 2 hours = 120 min, and 0.5 hour = 30 min. 120 + 30 = 150 minutes!
